title: The spider's web (344–350)
hookLine: those caught in passion run down the stream like a spider down the web it spun

cards: Watch a spider some morning. It builds the web out of itself, thread by thread, and then it lives there, running back and forth along the same lines it made.
The web is its home and its trap at once, and from the inside it never looks like a trap. People do this too. A grudge rehearsed for years.
A story about who you are. A routine built to feel safe that now keeps you small. Today's verses hold up the spider.

teach.b: These verses start with a man who has left the forest of desire and then runs straight back into it. Look at him, the text says: free, and running back into the chains. Then a surprise about chains.
The wise don't call a fetter strong if it's made of iron, wood or rope. Far stronger is the grip of longing for jewels, for family, for possessions. It hangs loose, and it's very hard to undo.
Then the spider, in verse three hundred forty-seven.
Those caught up in passion run down the stream of their desires the way a spider runs down the web it made itself. The key word is itself.
Nobody else spun this web, and that's the hopeful part: what you spun, you can step out of. Once they cut it, the verse says, the wise leave the world behind, free of care.
The next verse comes with a story from the commentary.
Uggasena, a rich young man, fell in love with an acrobat and became one himself.

One day, balanced at the top of a tall bamboo pole in front of a crowd, he heard the Buddha say: let go of what's before, let go of what's behind, let go of what's in between, and cross to the far shore.
According to the story, he understood right there on the pole.

The chapter ends with the restless mind, tossed by doubt, whose thirst keeps growing, and the calm mind that delights in quieting its thoughts and cuts the fetter. The web is real. So is the edge of it.

how: Buddhist teachers often tell the commentary's story of Uggasena the acrobat with verse 348, and use the spider image to show that craving builds its own trap; practice aims to see the web and let it go.

o: a safety net that keeps you from falling
a web spun by your own craving that traps you
a trap other people set to catch you

games.q: match each piece of today's verses and story.
p: runs down the web it made itself
the acrobat on the bamboo pole
what verse 348 says to let go

s: the verses say iron chains are the strongest fetters
longing for jewels, family and possessions binds harder.
the web in verse 347 is spun by the spider itself
that's the point: what you spun, you can step out of.
in the story, Uggasena understood while balanced on a pole
the commentary says he heard verse 348 at the top of a bamboo pole.

games.q: you're Uggasena, balanced at the top of a bamboo pole in front of a crowd. the Buddha speaks to you. what does he say?
o: climb down carefully and come to the monastery.
let go of before, behind and between, and cross over.
games.why: he said let go of what's before, behind and in between, and cross to the far shore; the story says Uggasena understood right there on the pole.

practice: Picture a spider's web in the morning light, beaded with dew, and think of one small web of your own, a story you tell yourself, a grudge, a routine that no longer helps, and see the threads you spun.
Then, like Uggasena on his pole, let go of what's behind, the past of it, what's ahead, the worry about it, and even what's in between. Just this breath, resting at the edge of the web.

wordCard.voice: Jāla. A net, a web: we run along webs of desire we spun ourselves, and what we spun, we can step out of.

orig.note: Pali jāla: a net, a web; verse 347 pictures the web the spider spun itself.

carryVoice: Your line: step out of the web. Nobody else holds the threads. That's day two hundred twenty.
